I'm Yamini, Vaibhav's younger sister, and I was the one the hospital called at 1 am. He had skidded his scooter into a divider on the ring road. A cracked wrist and stitches above his eye, the doctor said. Lucky.
When Papa walked into the ward, he didn't shout. He just stood at the foot of the bed and cried, which I had never seen him do.
For two years Vaibhav had said the drinking was "just weekends", "just stress", "under control". That night he said none of it. He stared at the plaster on his wrist and whispered, "I could have killed someone." Then, "I can't stop, Yamu. I've tried."
He looked more scared and more tired than I had ever seen him. I don't know exactly what was going on inside him. But I knew the door was open, maybe only for tonight. I sat on the bed and said, "Okay. Then we get help. Tomorrow. Together."

Friday, 5 March. Keerthana's manager called her into the glass cabin. The third missed client meeting, the late mornings, the smell. "We're letting you go." She argued: it was the new project, the traffic, anyone would be tired. At home she told Sahil it was office politics and opened a bottle.
Sunday, 7 March. She woke on the sofa at noon and found Sahil at the table with the bank statements, very quiet. "We can't pay rent next month," he said. "And I found the bottles in the shoe rack." She started to say, "It's not—" and stopped. Her hands were shaking. She was so tired of explaining.
Monday, 8 March. She sat on the edge of the bed, frightened in a way she couldn't name. "Sahil, I think I have a problem. A real one."
He put his arm around her. "Thank you for saying it. Let's call someone today, before either of us talks ourselves out of it."

qa.a: In the shoe rack.

Chinmay, you want to know when I stopped drinking? It wasn't when I decided to. It was when I got fired.
I was twenty-five. My manager called me in on a Monday. "Lokesh, you've come in smelling of alcohol three times. I can't cover for you any more." I walked home in the rain, still telling myself it was just bad luck.
Then I walked in, and my mother was sitting there. She'd heard. She didn't shout. She just cried, silently. I had never seen her cry like that.
Something cracked, beta. I sat on the floor and said, "Amma, I think I have a problem." I was so tired. So afraid.
She held my hand and said, "Then tomorrow, we go to the doctor." And we did.

qa.a: Young Lokesh felt exhausted and afraid, the denial cracking at the sight of Amma crying.

Rent was due on Friday, the monsoon had flooded the ground floor, and on Wednesday Yamini was fired. "Too many missed mornings," her manager said. "And you were seen at the bar at lunch again."
She walked home through ankle-deep water, still thinking, it's not that bad, everyone drinks. Then she saw Francis at the door, looking at her soaked, shaking figure.
"Yamini. What happened?"
And suddenly she couldn't hold it. "I got fired. Because of drinking. I've been lying to you for months. I'm so tired, Francis."
Francis didn't say "I knew it." He took her wet bag and said, "Come inside. We'll find help together. Tonight, if you want."

qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she finally told Francis?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and afraid, her denial breaking under the shock of being fired.

passage: The scooter lay on its side near the Lajpat Nagar flyover, one mirror snapped off. Tarun sat on the kerb with a scraped palm, a traffic policeman writing something down, and the smell of last night still on his breath at eleven in the morning. Dolma, his flatmate, arrived in an auto twelve minutes after his call. She didn't shout. She knelt, looked at his hand and said, "Your mother called me twice. She was crying." Something in Tarun gave way. All the lines he had used for a year, it's just weekends, everyone drinks, I'm fine at work, simply weren't there. "I'm scared, Dolma," he said. "I'm so tired of this." Dolma sat down on the kerb beside him. "Okay. Then today we tell her, and today we call someone who can help."
